title: Trump Ordered Strikes on Iran About Three Hours After Criticizing Nuclear Talks

About three hours later, aboard Air Force One, he ordered Operation Epic Fury. The Associated Press chronology also reported that Trump discussed the choice with Republican lawmakers on the flight. Oman’s foreign minister later said a deal had been within reach. The sequence establishes timing and competing assessments, not that Trump deliberately used his remarks to prepare the public for war.
description_long: The Associated Press timeline places Trump’s public criticism of Iran’s nuclear talks and his order for military action on the same afternoon, Feb. 27, 2026. At 12:25 p.m., he said he was unhappy with the negotiations but had not made a final decision. At 3:38 p.m., while flying to Texas, he directed the launch of Operation Epic Fury. During the flight, he asked a small group of Republican lawmakers for feedback; they discussed continuing talks versus striking, with the participants generally viewing negotiations as delay tactics, according to a person familiar with the discussion. Oman’s foreign minister, who had helped mediate, later said a deal had been within reach and expressed dismay that diplomacy was interrupted. This chronology shows a rapid public sequence and contrasting views of the talks. It does not establish that Trump’s earlier comments were intended to normalize escalation or that every diplomatic option had been exhausted.

It also collected differing remarks about regime change, threats to intervene during Iranian protests, missile risks and the war’s objectives. The report provides a record of public statements, not proof that mission boundaries or oversight changed.
description_long: The Associated Press’s March 2, 2026, compilation assembled statements from Trump and senior officials about Iran over the preceding eight months. After U.S. strikes in June 2025, Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the White House said Iran’s nuclear facilities or ability to make a weapon had been destroyed. Before the February 2026 strikes, officials again cited nuclear and ballistic-missile threats. The article also compared Trump’s changing comments on regime change: in June 2025 he floated it publicly while Vice President JD Vance said the administration did not seek it; on March 2, Hegseth said the operation was not a regime-change war, then noted that the regime had changed. The compilation included Trump’s January statements about protecting Iranian protesters and his later account that killings and planned executions had stopped. These examples document shifts and contradictions in public explanations. They do not identify a single formal mission baseline that was later abandoned or establish how the differences affected oversight.

title: Hennepin County Investigated 17 Alleged Incidents Involving Federal Immigration Agents
description_medium: On March 2, 2026, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said her office was examining 17 incidents of possible unlawful conduct by federal immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge. Publicly identified examples included Greg Bovino’s use of chemical irritants near Mueller Park and agents’ actions outside Roosevelt High School. Moriarty invited residents to submit video, photographs and eyewitness accounts. The announcement set out a state inquiry and a disputed question of federal immunity; it did not establish that an agent committed a crime or that a Trump directive caused the conduct.
description_long: Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced an investigation into 17 incidents involving federal immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge, the federal enforcement campaign in the Twin Cities. The Minnesota Star Tribune reported that two examples under review were Border Patrol official Greg Bovino’s use of a chemical irritant near Mueller Park on Jan. 21 and agents’ actions toward students at Roosevelt High School on Jan. 7. Moriarty launched the Transparency and Accountability Project so residents could submit photos, video and eyewitness accounts. She said her office would pursue charges where appropriate and that federal authorities had not supplied information about agents’ actions. The Department of Homeland Security argued that officers acting within their duties were immune from state liability. Moriarty disputed the idea of absolute immunity. The investigation concerned potential unlawful conduct, not an established pattern of criminal behavior. Its announcement did not determine whether individual incidents were lawful, whether charges would follow, or whether Trump personally directed the tactics being examined.

title: Hennepin County Opened a Criminal Inquiry Into Federal Agents’ Conduct During Operation Metro Surge
description_medium: Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said on March 2, 2026, that prosecutors were reviewing 17 incidents involving federal immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge. She named possible conduct near Mueller Park and Roosevelt High School and asked the public to share evidence through a county portal. Moriarty said state charges could be considered where warranted; DHS argued federal agents were immune from state liability when acting in their official roles. The inquiry was open, and no finding against an agent was announced.
description_long: The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office opened a review of 17 alleged incidents involving federal immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge. At a March 2 news conference, Mary Moriarty said the office was seeking public evidence, including photos, video and witness accounts, through a new portal. Two examples she identified were the use of chemical irritants near a Minneapolis park and agents’ actions at Roosevelt High School. Moriarty said that potential charges would require careful legal work because federal officers may claim immunity under the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause. The Department of Homeland Security asserted that officers acting within their duties were immune from state-level liability; Moriarty said there was no absolute immunity. The legal disagreement remained unresolved at the time. The investigation illustrates a state prosecutor’s effort to review alleged conduct by federal officers, but it does not establish that the agents acted unlawfully or that the inquiry changed the legitimacy of Trump’s immigration policy.

title: Federal Appeals Court Rejected a 90-Day Delay in the Tariff Refund Process
description_medium: On March 2, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit rejected the Trump administration’s request to wait 90 days before moving ahead on tariff refunds. The appeals court sent the next phase to the U.S. Court of International Trade, which would decide how claims should proceed. The ruling did not itself issue refunds or specify recipients and amounts.
description_long: The Federal Circuit on March 2, 2026, refused the Justice Department’s request to delay the next step in tariff-refund litigation for 90 days. The request followed the Supreme Court’s Feb. 20 ruling that invalidated tariffs imposed under emergency-powers authority; the high court had not explained how refunds should be handled. The appeals court sent the matter to the U.S. Court of International Trade in New York to determine the process. The decision removed the administration’s requested pause, but it did not establish the timing or total fiscal effect of future refunds.
